analysis.one_liner: Creates a pilot federal jobs guarantee, offering a job with benefits to anyone who wants one in high-unemployment areas.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in February 2026 with 4 cosponsors, was referred to two House committees and has had no further action while Congress remains in session.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have the Labor Department run a pilot program giving grants to up to 15 local governments, Tribal entities, or combinations of them in areas where unemployment is at least 50% higher than the national rate. Each program must offer a job to any adult resident who applies, pay at least the prevailing wage (or a higher local or union wage), include health coverage comparable to what federal employees get, and provide paid family and sick leave. Federal money for each pilot ends after three years, and the bill directs a rigorous evaluation of results. It also expands an existing employer tax credit to companies that hire people who spent at least three months in one of these programs.
analysis.who_benefits: Adults in participating high-unemployment areas who want a job: the program must hire anyone who applies, at no less than the prevailing wage, with health insurance comparable to federal employees' coverage, paid family and sick leave, and access to supports like child care, transportation, and training. Local economies also gain work on child care, elder and disability care, clean energy, and infrastructure projects, and employers get a new tax credit for hiring program participants after three months.

how_it_helps.text: Participating areas must offer a job to every adult resident who applies, for the duration of the pilot.

Program jobs must pay at least the greater of the prevailing wage, the applicable collective bargaining wage, or the higher of the federal or local minimum, and include health coverage comparable to the Federal Employee Health Benefits Program.
Programs must provide paid family leave and paid sick leave consistent with prior Congress bills (S. 1714 and S. 1664 of the 118th) if enacted, plus applicable state law.

Grant funds may pay for supportive services such as transportation, child care, dependent care, and housing assistance, plus adult education, job training, reentry help for people with records, and financial literacy.

Program jobs count within existing bargaining units and are covered by applicable collective bargaining agreements, and grant funds may not be used to displace existing employees or disrupt existing contracts.
The bill expands the Work Opportunity Tax Credit so employers hiring someone with at least 3 months in a job guarantee program can claim the credit for workers starting after December 31, 2026.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through an open-ended appropriation ('such sums as may be necessary') into a new Job Guarantee Program Trust Fund. Critics of job guarantee pilots also note a broader cost risk: if pilots are judged successful, permanent nationwide programs would be a large ongoing federal expense, and employers could face pressure if the guaranteed job sets a wage-and-benefits floor.

drawbacks.text: The funding is open-ended: the bill appropriates 'such sums as may be necessary' rather than capping spending, which makes the total federal cost unpredictable.

It is only a small pilot: grants go to no more than 15 eligible entities, federal funding for each ends after three years, and only areas with unemployment at least 150% of the national rate qualify, so most of the country would see no direct effect.

The wage floor is partly written by reference to bills from the prior Congress (S. 2488, S. 1714, S. 1664 of the 118th) that may never have been enacted, leaving gaps that would fall back on prevailing or state wages.

Defenders would acknowledge the three-year sunset and small scale mean the pilot cannot guarantee jobs nationwide, and the evaluation is retrospective, so someone seeking work outside the 15 pilot sites gets nothing from this bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For residents of the participating areas, the offer is strong: a guaranteed job at no less than the prevailing wage with federal-employee-level health coverage and paid leave. The main honest objections are fiscal design and scale: the open-ended appropriation makes the cost unpredictable, and a 15-site, three-year pilot is too small to move the national employment picture, so its real value is the evidence it generates for a future, larger decision.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Education and Workforce and Ways and Means committees, and neither committee has taken it up yet.

narrative.text: Representative Watson Coleman introduced the bill on February 12, 2026, joined by Representatives Omar, Lee of Pennsylvania, and McIver.
On the day of introduction, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce and, in addition, to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
Four Democratic representatives are listed as cosponsors; no Republicans are listed.
The bill has received no further action — no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote — since its referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet: the bill sits in two committees with no scheduled action, so the status quo — no federal jobs guarantee pilot, and no change for low-wage employers or taxpayers — continues while Congress stays in session.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; it awaits committee action

for.name: Bonnie Watson Coleman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Federal Jobs Guarantee Development Act of 2026 in the House.

for.name: Ilhan Omar, Summer Lee, and LaMonica McIver
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's three additional cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats (4 of 217 House Democrats) are listed as sponsors or cosponsors; no Republican has signed on, and no vote has occurred to reveal where either party stands.

industries.note: The bill expands the Work Opportunity Tax Credit to employers who hire participants after three months in the program, a subsidy on top of a program that would establish a wage-and-benefits floor. Employers get the tax credit; workers get the guaranteed job.
The bill routes up to 8 weeks of paid training through the public workforce system and funds adult education and literacy activities, including through public libraries.

Program jobs must be included in existing bargaining units where similarly situated employees are represented, and grant funds cannot be used to replace or displace existing employees or disrupt collective bargaining agreements.

industries.industry: Child care and elder/disability care providers
industries.note: The Secretary must designate child care and care for seniors and people with disabilities as national job priorities, creating paid public work in sectors with unmet demand; supportive-services funds also pay for child care for participants.
Clean energy jobs and sustainable infrastructure are named national job priorities, and energy and infrastructure jobs must not worsen climate impacts.

analysis.trajectory: With no cosponsors beyond the original four, no committee action two months after referral, and the bill split between two committees, its realistic path is to die quietly at the end of the 119th Congress without a markup or vote, like most bills referred to committee. A jobs guarantee at this scale would be a major federal spending commitment, which makes early GOP-run committee consideration unlikely; its best plausible use is as a template for a larger future majority.
